value.lead: A framework for running any medical practice as a business. It is organized by what has to be managed, not by one vendor's product list: **13 domains**, each broken into areas with what good looks like, where it usually breaks, what to do, and what to measure.
how_to_use: Pick a domain. Each one opens into its areas.
In an area, read *What good looks like* against your own practice, then the questions. Honest answers are the assessment.
Use *What to measure* for the definition, the formula and a benchmark. Where no reliable public benchmark exists, the page says so instead of inventing one.
Open **My practice** to see every area already judged for this practice, with its numbers, risks and next steps.
value.method: The domain list follows the recognized bodies of knowledge for practice management (the MGMA Body of Knowledge, HFMA MAP Keys, the OIG compliance program guidance, the NCQA medical-home concepts and the Medicare quality program) and was checked against the 60 documents of a purchased vendor library. Rules are cited to the regulation or CMS manual. Benchmarks are cited to their source with the data year, and labelled when they are convention and not measurement.

value.lead: The universal framework applied to this practice, using its own financial statements, billing data and public Medicare data. **The practice is profitable and its billing machinery is fast, though two faults were found in it on November 10, 2026. Its main problems are untested billing patterns, coverage and enrollment gaps, the risk of a cut from Medicare's quality program, and dependence on one physician.**
headline: **Profitable and lean.** $585,057 before owner pay on $1,058,153 of revenue in the last twelve months. Operating cost is 44.7% of revenue.

**Worth about $300,000 today** as a business (range about $50,000 to $680,000). Buyers pay for the profit left after a physician is paid a market wage for this workload. That profit is about $88,000 a year. This is a planning estimate. It depends most on that wage and on how the billing reviews come out.

**The largest money on the table is place of service, and the owner's rule for it is live.** Until November 10, 2026 every care-management line in the five nursing buildings went out as a skilled stay. For long-term residents the correct code pays more in 2026: Medicare allows $142.98 against $80.71 for the first hour of complex care management. Since November 10 billing's rule enters these lines under the long-term code. Care management is billed at month end, so November's lines will be the first to carry it, and whether the billing system keeps the new code has not been checked yet. That is worth an estimated $50,000 to $70,000 a year of Medicare payment. Each facility's list of residents in a Medicare Part A stay is still the proof.

**Two billing patterns still need a chart review before anyone else asks:** visit levels far above national patterns, and advance care planning billed with no tested record of time. A third needs the owner's decision: the charge import entered 149 October visits under the other clinician. The owner settled the 15 charge lines not yet billed on November 10, 2026; the 152 lines already billed are still open. New claims follow the owner's rules of November 10, 2026 for place of service and for initial nursing facility visits; the initial-visit rule is right only when the physician personally does the visit. On those two points past claims are not being reopened.

**Money is leaking before and after the claim goes out.** On November 10, 2026, 122 visits from the charge feed had no claim: $26,373 of charges, which is not a forecast of payment. 84 of them ($18,802) could never bill because of a software fault found and proven that day. The fix went live on November 11, 2026; the 84 visits themselves have not been sent yet. They go out on the terms the owner approved: one test visit first, and 71 of them only if a coverage check dated to the visit shows the plan active. 30% of recent claim lines paid nothing, and two thirds of those carry one denial code, the one Medicare gives most often on care-management lines. $342,620 is open with 35% older than 90 days.

**Dated items:** file the physician's Medicaid renewal by November 13, after resetting the Medicaid portal password (December 1 is the last call; the agreement expires December 27, 2026). For Medicare's quality program, where an estimated cut of about 9% of 2028 Medicare payments is at stake: the registration can be changed only until November 30; name the one improvement activity by December 15; renew the rule that adds the advance care plan code to Medicare claims before January 1, because billing adds it only to visits dated in 2026 (calendar entry December 21); and attest the activity between January 4 and March 31, 2027. Salary and owner-loan decisions with the accountant are needed before December 31. Medicare claims that were never accepted expire one year after the date of service, so some from late 2025 expire each week.

**First four moves for the owner:** get each nursing facility's list of residents in a Medicare Part A stay to back the new place-of-service code, decide this week what to do with the October visits entered under the other clinician, engage a healthcare attorney before the visit-level audit starts, and file the Medicaid renewal by November 13. Three short items on the work list are due sooner still: replace the database access key that was shared in a chat (due November 10), turn off open sign-up to this application (November 11) and pause the automatic write-off of old balances (November 12).

value.lead: Patterns in the practice's own billing data that an auditor's software would also see, set beside the rule each one touches. **A pattern is a reason to look at charts. It is not a finding that anything was billed wrongly.**
how_to_use: Read the findings in order. Critical and high come first.

Engage a healthcare attorney first, so that the reviews of past visit claims are directed by counsel. Place of service on new claims follows the owner's rule since November 10, 2026; get each facility's list of residents in a Medicare Part A stay to back it. Do not move visit levels up or down to match national averages. The note for that day decides the level.

The billing database holds claims, not clinical notes. The findings on billing patterns still have to be tested against the charts: visit levels and advance care planning first, then who saw each patient on the October visits entered under the other clinician. Place of service is tested against each facility's Part A list, and the 84 never-billed visits are a software fault proven from the billing records. The last finding, on care-management claims, is not up for review. The owner confirmed on November 10, 2026 that consent, care plans and time records are on file for these claims.

When a review that the attorney directs is finished, its result goes to the attorney, not into this application. On the work list record only that the step is complete, and the date. For the other reviews, record the result and the date on the work list.
value.foot: Management information and education, not legal or coding advice. If a chart review shows Medicare was overpaid, federal law requires reporting and returning the money within 60 days of identifying it. A prompt, good-faith review of related claims pauses those 60 days, for no more than 180 days after the first overpayment was identified.

value.lead: The purchased CleanClaimRx library and every issue of the vendor's free newsletter, read in full and scored. It was used as an outline to make sure the universal framework misses nothing, and every rule or number it states was treated as unverified until found in a primary source.
verdict: **60 documents, 2,566 pages, list price $1,032 for the bundles bought.** Every document was written by an AI system with no named author, sources or dates on its numbers.
**Quality, scored 1 to 5 after reading each document in full:** 1 scored 1, 29 scored 2, 30 scored 3. None scored 4 or 5.
**Best use:** as a checklist of topics and worksheets. The operating routines (daily queues, root-cause logs, reconciliation steps) are sound and transfer to any practice.
**Do not rely on it for rules or numbers.** Benchmarks are unsourced, several code and deadline statements are wrong, and almost nothing addresses Medicare facility-based billing.
**All 445 rules and numbers extracted from the documents were checked against primary sources.** 212 partly, 94 contradicted, 74 supported, 44 unverifiable, 21 outdated.

**The vendor's free newsletter was read too: 21 issues published from May to November 2026.** Quality: 11 scored 2, 10 scored 3. Of 105 news claims checked against the original announcement or rule: 29 supported, 55 partly, 8 contradicted, 3 outdated, 10 unverifiable. It is where the vendor reports dated news (new rules, deadlines, payer announcements), which the purchased documents lack. Each item is checked in the table below.
